title: Adjusting Construction Contract Prices 2026: When Is It Allowed?
desc: When a construction contract price can be adjusted in 2026: change of scope, force majeure, unusual material price rises, variations under Decree 210.
summary: The cases in which a construction contract price may be amended or adjusted under the Construction Law 2025 and Decree 210/2026/ND-CP, and how to handle material price swings or variations.
body: p

Steel and cement prices rise mid-project, the owner wants an extra room, excavation meets weak soil... all raise the question: can the contract price be adjusted? The answer lies in Article 84 of the Construction Law 2025 and Section 2 of Decree 210/2026/ND-CP.
h2
1. Cases in which a contract may be amended
p

Amending a contract includes adjusting quantities, schedule, time, unit prices and the contract price; it must be done in writing and while the contract is still in effect. The parties may agree to amend when (Clauses 1 and 2, Article 84):
ul
The State changes policy or law directly affecting the contract.
There is a change in the content or scope of work, techniques, quality, schedule, or conditions for advances and payment.
A force majeure event occurs.
There is a fundamental change of circumstances.
Other cases agreed by the parties in accordance with law.
h2
2. Whether the price changes depends on the contract type
ul

Lump sum: the price does not change throughout the contract, except for force majeure, fundamental change of circumstances, change of scope of work or other cases agreed by the parties (Point a, Clause 2, Article 6).
Fixed unit price: unit prices do not change, but payment is based on the actual accepted quantities (Point b, Clause 2, Article 6).
Adjustable unit price: unit prices and the contract price are adjusted as agreed in the contract (Point c, Clause 2, Article 6).
p

The adjustment method and formula are agreed by the parties in the contract, or a formula under international practice may be applied (Clause 3, Article 22). If the contract does not state how to adjust, it is very hard to claim a price increase later.
h2
3. Unusual material price rises
p

Under Clause 3, Article 18 of Decree 210/2026/ND-CP, when price movements are unusual and beyond what could be forecast at signing, and may cause serious loss to a party, the parties must analyse the impact (quantities done, quantities remaining, losses if continuing or terminating) and check against Article 13 of the Construction Law to decide on amending the contract, ensuring risk sharing between the two sides.
p

A fundamental change of circumstances must meet all the conditions of Article 420 of the Civil Code: an objective cause arising after signing; it could not have been foreseen; the change is so great that, had it been known, the contract would not have been signed or would have been signed on entirely different terms; continued performance would cause serious loss; and the affected party has applied all necessary measures. The affected party may then require renegotiation; if no agreement is reached, it may ask the Court to terminate or amend the contract.
h2
4. Variations outside the contract
p

The parties agree specifically on the cases and procedure for adjusting quantities (Clause 1, Article 23). For reasonable variation quantities, the two sides must agree the unit price or the principle for determining it before doing the work, as the basis for amending the contract (Clause 3, Article 23). This is the most common source of disputes in housing: the owner asks for extra work orally, and at final settlement the parties cannot agree on the price.
h2
5. Separate rules for public-investment and PPP projects
p

For contracts in public-investment and PPP projects, where the actual quantity increases or decreases by more than 20% of the contract quantity, and also changes the contract price by more than 0.25% and the unit price of that work by 1%, a new unit price is determined; for increases or decreases of 20% or less, the contract unit price is kept (Clause 2, Article 24). Private housing may refer to this approach when drafting the contract.
h2
6. What the homeowner should do
ol
Choose a suitable contract price type and state clearly the cases in which adjustment is allowed.
State the price source and price index used for adjustment (if any).
Every variation must have a document or appendix stating the quantity and unit price before construction.
When there is an unusual price movement, give written notice and propose a way of handling it (Clause 4, Article 18).
note

This article is a summary for reference only and does not replace the legal texts. The 20% threshold and the 7-working-day response procedure are mandatory only for public-investment and PPP projects; private housing contracts are mainly governed by the parties' agreement and the Civil Code.
